title: ⭐ Practice: a day that begins with a connection

questions.prompt: Four words of this lesson, and the four definitions this lesson gives them. Match each word with the definition that belongs to it.

options.text: bullying
logging on
texting
bustle
writing on the computer
frightening or hurting a weaker person
moving about in a busy way, as a whole crowd does
connecting a computer to a system

questions.explanation: Take them one at a time and ask what each word is for. Connecting a computer to a system is the gesture that opens the school day at nine: that is logging on, and it is done and over the moment the connection holds. Writing on that computer is what fills the lesson once the connection is there: that is texting, and it goes on all morning - one is the door, the other is what goes on behind it. The other two never name the same thing and must never be swapped. Frightening or hurting somebody weaker is deliberate, and it is the work of one person, or of three: that is bullying. Moving about in a busy way is nobody's fault and holds no cruelty at all - a corridor can be full of it without a single unkind child in it: that is bustle, and a pupil can flee a corridor full of it without anybody having been unkind to him.

questions.prompt: A pupil writes in his notebook: "The main appeal of a virtual school is that nobody stares at you when you get an answer wrong." What is he saying about virtual schools?

options.text: that is what makes a virtual school attractive to him
that is what a virtual school asks of the pupils it takes
that is what a virtual school forbids its pupils to do
that is what he finds hardest to bear in a virtual school

questions.explanation: In this lesson the word names attractiveness: whatever it is about a thing that draws people towards it. Ask what the appeal of something is and you are asking why anybody would want it. So the sentence is telling you the reason this pupil is drawn to a school of that kind, and it is a reason Natalie would have recognised at once. What the school asks of him would need a different word entirely, since nothing here is being demanded of anybody. Nothing is being forbidden either, and reading the sentence as a complaint turns a good reason into a grievance and gets the boy exactly backwards.

questions.prompt: A report says: "In January 2006 Shan Jayran and her husband John Davies opened First College, an on-line high school, and now it has twenty-two students." A pupil writes in his notes: "Twenty-two children have enrolled at First College since it opened." Why is that not what the report said?

options.text: the figure counts the students the college has now, not everyone who ever enrolled
the figure counts the students who log on each morning, and not those whose names are on the roll
the figure counts the two people who opened the college as well
the figure counts the students of every on-line high school together

questions.explanation: A number heard on the radio always comes with a moment attached, spoken or understood, and the little word now is that moment here. It tells you the size of the college on the day the journalist spoke, and says nothing whatever about the years between the opening and that day: pupils may have come and gone without leaving a trace in the sentence. Nor does the report count anybody's morning connection - it is talking about who belongs to the college, not who has switched a machine on. The founders are named as founders and never counted among the students, and the college the sentence describes is one college, opened by two named people, not a total for the country.

questions.prompt: On the timetable of an on-line high school, two expressions are printed inside inverted commas, and nothing else on the grid is: at nine the pupils chat to classmates in the "school hall", and at two the day ends on "home time". Why those two expressions, and no others?

options.text: there is no hall to stand in and no journey home: the words are on loan
those two moments are the only ones a pupil is actually allowed to miss
those two words are the ones the pupils are asked to learn by heart
the hall and the front door are the two places a whole school would share

questions.explanation: Nobody puts break or lunch between inverted commas, because a break is a break wherever you take it. But a school that exists only where its pupils' computers meet owns no room they could all stand in, and at two o'clock nobody sets off anywhere: they have been at home since the connection was made. Both expressions were lifted from a school built of bricks and set to work here, and the inverted commas are the writer owning up to the loan. They are not a warning that the moment is optional, they are not a reading list, and they cannot be pointing at shared rooms in a building that does not exist.

questions.prompt: In a debate one pupil says: "Nothing at all happens in those schools before half past nine." The other answers, raising his voice on one word: "They do chat to their classmates from nine o'clock." Why has he put that extra word into a sentence that was perfectly good without it?

options.text: to press on the truth of what he says, against the doubt just raised
to say that they chat far more often than his opponent seems to believe
to put his sentence into a tense his opponent had not used
to turn his sentence into a question about his opponent's claim

questions.explanation: Take the extra word out and the sentence still stands and still means the same: it was never needed to build anything. It was chosen, and it is chosen for one reason - somebody has just denied what the speaker is about to assert, and the speaker is answering that denial head on. The sense added is it is true that, not more often, not for longer and not more than anyone else, which is why an answer about frequency misses it. The tense has not moved either, since both speakers are talking about what happens every morning. And nothing here is being asked: this is a flat contradiction, delivered with the voice lifting on the small word that carries it.

questions.prompt: A class draws two columns on the board, one headed benefits of virtual schools and the other headed drawbacks, and sorts into them what the report said. Which of these belongs under drawbacks?

options.text: five hours a day in the same chair, and the side-effects that follow
a pupil who was bullied no longer meets the ones who bullied him
a pupil who was afraid to speak in class no longer sits in one
a pupil enrols once, and after that has only to log on each morning

questions.explanation: Sort them with a single question: is this something the pupil gains, or something the pupil pays? Escaping the boys who took his lunch is a gain. Never having to face the class that frightened her is a gain. A single enrolment followed by a daily connection is a convenience, and it is the machinery the report calls light. Only one line names a price, and the report states it aloud: a body kept in one chair from nine until two, with the aching back and tired eyes that come with it. Note where the figure comes from - the school's own grid, not from anybody arguing against it.

questions.prompt: A visitor claims that the pupils of an on-line high school never speak to one another. A pupil wants to answer him with the emphatic form, and to change nothing else in the sentence "They chat in the school hall every morning." Which sentence does that?

options.text: They do chat in the school hall every morning.
They did chat in the school hall every morning.
They do chat in the school hall far more often than he thinks.
They really chat in the school hall every morning.

questions.explanation: The auxiliary has to agree with the subject and with the moment, and nothing else in the line may move. A plural subject takes do, and the verb behind it stays bare, since the auxiliary is now the word holding the person. Putting that auxiliary into the past answers a claim nobody made: the visitor is talking about what happens every morning, and the answer has to stay where he is. Adding how often they chat is a second way of leaving the line: the form insists that a thing is true, it never says that it happens more often, and the sentence it was asked to keep said every morning. And pressing a sentence with an adverb is not this form at all - what the lesson asks for is the auxiliary standing in front of the bare verb, which is exactly what the book's own example prints.
